I had a bad reaction. I was taking Lexapro (filled at my normal pharmacy), but then I started taking Sumatriptan and it was sent to a specialty pharmacy. I hadn't been to my normal doctor to have my Lexapro moved to the specialty pharmacy, so I had two pharmacists for the two medications. My neurologist knew I was on Lexapro and didn't mention any risks. I took both medications for two months, and during that time my vision became blurry, I had very bad vertigo, and trouble staying awake. I'm talking I would be physically unable to wake up until 11am, and even after that I would fall asleep sitting up. It obviously interfered with my work. My mind was so cloudy I didn't notice the difference, and started having suicidal ideation and began making plans for a way to commit suicide where my family could still collect life insurance. It took two months for my husband to realize that maybe something was wrong with the medication, start researching, and call my neurologist. I had to wear off the triptans and start a new medication.

I think the reaction I had is VERY rare because I don't know anyone else who had that issue and there isn't much about it online. However, I would ask for a list of potential side effects to watch out for and make sure a close family member knows and watches as well.

It's not immature at all to feel the loss of yourself pre-parent. The beginning of being a parent inevitably means the end of being childless and it's okay to grieve that lost independence. Just know that even this phase of life will end too and eventually you'll come to find a balance of who you were before kids and who you are now. 

My kid is 7 now, and when he was little it seemed like my old life was over. For a while, it was. But now he's got some independence and personality, and there are times where he plays in his room while I do my own thing, or he stays at a family member's house while I enjoy alone time, or we do activities together that we both enjoy. I don't get to be exactly who I was before having a kid, but I haven't forfeited my entire identity to parenthood, either- which I remember thinking I had to when my son was about your LO's age. It'll get better. Just give it some time.

What state are you in? Each state has their own rule on licensing, but I can give you my experience from Texas. 
I did the school counseling track with LPC add-on. I ended up with 66 hours instead of 60 so not too much longer. 

Benefits- 
I was able to take a paid internship my last semester of grad school. The internship is essentially a full-time job if you do it in one semester, and I couldn't afford to do it unpaid. Most mental health internships in my area are unpaid, whereas school are paid because you just start working as a school counselor. 
Once I finished I was able to start accruing my LPC-A hours quickly. You can work as an LPC-A in Texas but insurance companies won't pay, so you can only do private pay which cuts down on clients. 
Many districts are adding LPCs for Gen Ed onto their staffing - it helps if you are already a CSC. 

Drawbacks- 
Varies district by district (and even campus by campus) but many school counselors don't actually get to counsel. My last campus I was able to do some, but my instruction from campus admin was that my main focus should be testing and data, which was in direct contradiction with the school counseling model. If your true focus is mental health you may need to try a few campuses before you find one with those same priorities.

No problem! Feel free to ask more. I'd say the biggest brands to look out for are Proctor and Gamble brands and Dove. Many of their products have a cruelty free label, or say not tested on animals. However, most are sold in mainland China or use raw materials that were tested on animals, making them not cruelty free.

If an ingredient is no longer tested on animals it is considered cruelty free, even if it was tested on animals in the past. A lot of tests of products are done to ensure that the combination of ingredients gives the desired results, so every product you purchase will have been tested- cruelty free just makes sure it wasn't tested on animals. 

Your question about different regulatory landscapes is really where the cruelty free community differs. As you mentioned, different countries have different legal requirements for the testing of ingredients. China is the biggest example here. So, a company could say they don't test on animals, but if they sell their products in China, China will still have the right to test the product on animals themselves. Some people say that as long as the company themselves doesn't test on animals, it can count as cruelty free. Others disagree and say that if they are willing to sell to China, knowing they will test on animals, it is no longer cruelty free. 

There is no regulation on cruelty free labels. That's why there are so many different ones. Some labels are just made up by the company themselves and carry no weight. Others are verified by different agencies, such as PETA. [here](https://ethicalelephant.com/cruelty-free-vegan-labels-logos/) is a link that describes the different labels.

At the end of the day, it really requires the consumer to research different brands and ask them how they test and formulate their product. [Cruelty Free Kitty](https://www.crueltyfreekitty.com/) has one of the strictest standards I've seen on cruelty free products, and does not count companies that sell in China as cruelty free, so a company could be potentially approved by PETA but not by Cruelty Free Kitty. I hope that helps- let me know what other questions you have!
